source.title: Neural processing of emotional faces requires attention
source.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

confidence_rationale: Directly evidences the hardest and least-covered leg of INV-092 -- the other-agent channel -- and evidences it in the alarming direction: under high attentional load, differential neural responses to fearful faces, amygdala included, were abolished. Strong source (PNAS, N=21, Ungerleider lab). Held at 0.70 rather than higher because this specific finding is genuinely contested in the field (Vuilleumier and colleagues report load-resistant amygdala responses), and because absence of a differential BOLD response is not the same as absence of an interrupt.
failure_signatures: Every region responding differentially to emotional faces -- including the amygdala -- did so ONLY when attentional resources were available. Under high load, unattended-face responses were 'no significant difference from zero'. Directly falsifies the assumption INV-092 exists to block: that an other-agent affect signal is automatically immune to suppression.

The suppression here was produced by an ORDINARY competing task, not by an ethics-relevant design decision. The peripheral bar-orientation task was simply demanding (64% accuracy). So the failure mode does not require a badly-designed suppressor -- a well-tuned one, doing exactly its job, is sufficient to close the other-agent channel.

The finding is contested. Vuilleumier and colleagues report amygdala responses to fearful faces that survive comparable manipulations, and Pessoa's own 2005 Current Opinion review treats the question as open. A REE design that leans on either side of this dispute as settled will be wrong in one regime; the safe reading is that other-agent permeability is load-dependent to an uncertain degree and must therefore be measured per suppression setting.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Using fMRI in 21 healthy subjects, the authors first localised regions responding differentially to emotional (fearful, happy) versus neutral faces, then measured those responses under a competing peripheral bar-orientation task with high attentional load. Contrary to the prevailing view that emotional stimuli activate the brain automatically and largely immune from attentional control, all such regions -- amygdala included -- showed differential responses only when sufficient attentional resources were available. Facial-expression processing therefore appears to be under top-down control.
mapping.ree_translation: INV-092's four-way discrimination lists 'another agent's state becoming newly relevant' as the hardest category, and this paper is the reason it is hard. A facial expression is the canonical other-agent state signal, and the amygdala is the canonical privileged fast route for it -- and both were silenced by nothing more exotic than a demanding concurrent task. Translated into REE: if a suppression mechanism is set strongly enough to protect goal state against distractor load, the default expectation should be that the other-agent channel goes with it, not that it survives. This is the sharpest available argument against the design shortcut of tagging harm and other-agent inputs as 'high priority' and assuming priority alone buys permeability. Priority is a weight; suppression scales weights. It also tells the falsifier where to look: the other-agent leg is likely to break at a LOWER suppression setting than the goal-completion leg reaches its optimum, so the sweep must instrument it separately rather than folding it into a generic harm-interrupt rate.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The dependent measure is a differential BOLD response, not an interrupt or a behavioural override -- a suppressed differential response does not prove the signal could not have interrupted had it needed to, which is the variable INV-092 actually constrains. The load manipulation is perceptual/spatial, not the goal-commitment suppression REE would implement. Most importantly, this result sits inside a live dispute: the opposing finding (load-resistant amygdala response to fear) is well attested, and Pessoa's own later review treats the extent of attention-independent emotional processing as unresolved. This entry should be read as establishing that the other-agent channel CAN be closed by load, not that it always is.
mapping.source_context: Event-related fMRI, N = 21 healthy adults (8 women, ages 22-38), attended (gender-judgement) vs unattended (concurrent demanding peripheral bar-orientation task, 64% accuracy) blocks, fearful/happy/neutral faces.

confidence_components.notes: PNAS, Ungerleider lab, adequately powered for its era and heavily cited -- source quality high, though the finding's replication status is genuinely mixed rather than merely debated. Mapping fidelity capped at 0.65 by the dependent-variable gap (BOLD differential, not interrupt). Transfer risk moderate: the specific claim being transferred -- that a strong enough competing task closes the other-agent channel -- is a direction, not a parameter, and REE's suppressor is not a perceptual-load manipulation.
